The belief: a service is a singleton by nature. Wherever you provide it, Angular creates it once and hands the same object to everyone who asks.
Most of the time, that's exactly what you see. Nearly every service starts as
, and both mean one shared instance for the whole app. Tutorials call services singletons, and the docs describe root-provided services as a single, shared instance. On top of that,
containers you register a service once and it's available everywhere. In Angular, where you register it decides who shares it.
Angular doesn't have one container. It has a tree of
in two layers. Environment injectors hold app-level providers: the root one gets

gets its own injector, so this layer mirrors your component tree.
Lookup walks up and stops at the first match
, Angular first walks up the element injectors: the component's own, then its parent's, and so on toward the root component. Only if none of them provides
does it move on to the environment injectors, the route's and then root's. The first provider it finds wins, and the injector that holds it owns the instance.

An injector creates at most one instance per provider and reuses it. The root injector exists once, so a root-provided service behaves like an app-wide singleton. A component's injector exists once per component instance, so
